options.text: Maintenance of internal conditions within preset limits despite change
options.why: Homeostatic variables can fluctuate around set points. The control systems keep those fluctuations within tolerable limits.

options.text: Prevention of every change in the internal environment
options.why: Internal conditions do change. Preventing every fluctuation would be impossible and isn’t what homeostasis means.

options.text: Amplification of internal changes until a process finishes
options.why: That describes positive feedback, such as the amplification involved in childbirth. Homeostasis mainly uses negative feedback.

options.text: Maintenance of external conditions at one constant value
options.why: Homeostasis regulates the internal environment. It allows organisms to function despite changes outside the body.

questions.stem: What makes a feedback loop negative?

options.text: The response reduces the original deviation from the set point
options.why: The response opposes the change, so the regulated variable moves back toward its target range.

options.text: The response amplifies the original deviation from the set point
options.why: That describes positive feedback. Amplification moves the system farther from its starting condition until something else stops it.

options.text: The receptor prevents the regulated variable from changing
options.why: A receptor detects a change; it doesn’t prevent one. Effectors produce the corrective response.

options.text: The effector establishes a new set point after each change
options.why: An effector acts on the regulated variable. It normally returns the variable toward the existing set point.

questions.stem: Which response follows a rise in blood glucose concentration?

options.text: Beta cells release insulin, promoting glucose uptake and glycogenesis
options.why: Insulin signals target tissues to remove glucose from the blood and store some of it as glycogen.

options.text: Alpha cells release insulin, promoting glycogenolysis in the liver
options.why: Alpha cells release glucagon, not insulin. Glycogenolysis would raise blood glucose rather than lower it.

options.text: Beta cells release glucagon, promoting glucose release by the liver
options.why: Beta cells release insulin. Glucagon comes from alpha cells when blood glucose has fallen.

options.text: Liver cells release insulin, promoting glucose uptake by the pancreas
options.why: Pancreatic endocrine cells release insulin. The liver is a major target organ, not the source of this hormone.

questions.stem: Which change is the physiological basis of type 1 diabetes?

options.text: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
options.why: Loss of beta cells causes little or no insulin production, so insulin must be replaced.

options.text: Reduced sensitivity of target cells to insulin
options.why: That is insulin resistance, the characteristic early defect in type 2 diabetes.

options.text: Excessive secretion of glucagon after every meal
options.why: Glucagon regulation may be abnormal in diabetes, but this isn’t the defining cause of type 1 diabetes.

options.text: Failure of liver cells to store any glycogen
options.why: Poor glucose regulation affects glycogen storage, but type 1 diabetes starts with destruction of insulin-producing beta cells.

questions.stem: How does sweating lower core body temperature?

options.text: Evaporation transfers energy from the skin to water vapor
options.why: Water requires energy to evaporate. Taking that energy from the skin removes heat from the body.

options.text: Sweat conducts heat into the body’s deeper tissues
options.why: Moving heat deeper wouldn’t cool the body effectively. Cooling occurs when evaporating water carries energy away.

options.text: Sweat lowers the set point detected by thermoreceptors
options.why: Sweat changes heat loss, not the set point. Thermoreceptors then detect the resulting temperature change.

options.text: Evaporation stops blood from reaching skin capillaries
options.why: Sweating doesn’t stop skin blood flow. Vasodilation commonly increases that flow during heat stress.

questions.stem: How does uncoupled respiration in brown adipose tissue warm the body?

options.text: Energy from respiration is released as heat instead of being captured in as much ATP
options.why: Uncoupling proteins let the mitochondrial proton gradient dissipate, so more respiratory energy appears as heat.

options.text: ATP synthesis accelerates until ATP molecules raise the temperature of the blood
options.why: Uncoupling reduces the amount of ATP made from the proton gradient. The released energy becomes heat.

options.text: Stored lipids insulate mitochondria and prevent heat from leaving their membranes
options.why: Brown fat generates heat metabolically. Insulation is mainly a property of larger stores of white subcutaneous fat.

options.text: Brown fat contracts repeatedly in the same manner as shivering skeletal muscle
options.why: Shivering uses skeletal-muscle contractions. Brown adipose tissue produces heat through mitochondrial respiration without contracting.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes excretion from osmoregulation?

options.text: Excretion removes metabolic wastes; osmoregulation controls body-fluid osmotic concentration
options.why: The kidney performs both jobs, but waste removal and regulation of water and solute balance are different functions.

options.text: Excretion removes feces; osmoregulation removes urea from the blood
options.why: Loss of feces is egestion. Urea removal is an example of excretion, not the definition of osmoregulation.

options.text: Excretion controls blood water content; osmoregulation removes metabolic wastes
options.why: The definitions have been reversed. Water balance belongs to osmoregulation, while waste removal belongs to excretion.

options.text: Excretion occurs in nephrons; osmoregulation occurs only in the hypothalamus
options.why: The hypothalamus detects osmotic changes, but the kidneys alter water loss. Both processes involve the nephrons.

questions.stem: Why do blood cells normally remain in glomerular blood during ultrafiltration?

options.text: They are too large to cross the filtration barrier
options.why: The basement membrane and associated filtration structures allow water and small solutes through but retain cells and most large proteins.

options.text: They are actively transported back from Bowman’s capsule
options.why: Blood cells shouldn’t enter Bowman’s capsule in the first place. Their size prevents them from crossing the filtration barrier.

options.text: They have no metabolic value to proximal tubule cells
options.why: Ultrafiltration doesn’t sort substances by metabolic value. Size and pressure determine what crosses the barrier.

options.text: They move against the hydrostatic pressure in the glomerulus
options.why: Cells don’t actively swim against glomerular pressure. They remain because the filtration barrier excludes them.

questions.stem: Where is most filtered glucose normally reabsorbed?

options.text: The proximal convoluted tubule
options.why: Sodium-glucose cotransport in the proximal convoluted tubule normally recovers the filtered glucose.

options.text: The Bowman’s capsule
options.why: Bowman’s capsule receives glomerular filtrate. It isn’t the main site of selective glucose reabsorption.

options.text: The ascending limb of the loop of Henle
options.why: The ascending limb transports sodium ions and helps establish the medullary gradient. It isn’t the main glucose-recovery site.

options.text: The collecting duct
options.why: The collecting duct adjusts water reabsorption under ADH control. Glucose should have been recovered much earlier.

questions.stem: What is the relevant role of the ascending limb of the loop of Henle in this topic?

options.text: It actively transports sodium ions to maintain a high medullary osmotic concentration
options.why: The resulting medullary gradient later favors water movement out of collecting ducts.

options.text: It selectively reabsorbs all glucose by sodium-glucose cotransport
options.why: That mainly occurs in the proximal convoluted tubule. The ascending limb’s relevant role is establishing the medullary salt gradient.

options.text: It filters plasma proteins from blood into the nephron
options.why: Ultrafiltration occurs at the glomerulus, and most plasma proteins remain in the blood.

options.text: It inserts aquaporins into collecting-duct cell membranes
options.why: ADH triggers aquaporin insertion in collecting-duct cells. The loop of Henle establishes the osmotic gradient.

questions.stem: A dehydrated person has an increased blood osmotic concentration. Which response follows?

options.text: More ADH is released, increasing collecting-duct aquaporins and water reabsorption
options.why: More aquaporins make the collecting duct more permeable, so water moves out of the filtrate by osmosis.

options.text: Less ADH is released, increasing urine volume and lowering water reabsorption
options.why: That response would remove more water and worsen dehydration. Low ADH is appropriate when the blood is too dilute.

options.text: More insulin is released, causing water to enter liver cells
options.why: Insulin regulates blood glucose, not collecting-duct water permeability. ADH is the relevant hormone here.

options.text: Less glucagon is released, causing aquaporins to leave intracellular vesicles
options.why: Glucagon regulates blood glucose and doesn’t control collecting-duct aquaporins. ADH controls their membrane location.

questions.stem: What urine would be expected when ADH concentration is low?

options.text: A large volume of dilute urine
options.why: Fewer aquaporins remain in collecting-duct membranes, so less water is reabsorbed and more stays in the urine.

options.text: A small volume of concentrated urine
options.why: That is produced when ADH is high and collecting ducts reabsorb more water.

options.text: Urine containing many plasma proteins
options.why: ADH changes water reabsorption. Plasma proteins are normally excluded earlier by the glomerular filtration barrier.

options.text: Urine containing no urea or ions
options.why: Low ADH changes urine water content, not the need to excrete urea and some dissolved ions.

questions.stem: Which blood-flow pattern is expected during vigorous exercise?

options.text: Increased flow to skeletal muscle, reduced flow to gut and kidneys, stable cerebral flow
options.why: Blood is redirected toward active muscle while brain supply is protected and less urgent digestive and renal activity receives a smaller share.

options.text: Reduced flow to skeletal muscle, increased flow to gut and kidneys, stable cerebral flow
options.why: That pattern conflicts with the high oxygen demand of active muscle. Gut and renal flow commonly decrease during vigorous exercise.

options.text: Increased flow to every organ because cardiac output rises uniformly
options.why: Higher cardiac output doesn’t mean equal increases everywhere. Arteriole diameter redistributes the available blood.

options.text: Increased flow only to the brain because it controls skeletal-muscle contraction
options.why: The brain remains supplied, but active muscles need a large increase in oxygen and respiratory substrates.

questions.stem: A substance is present in blood plasma and glomerular filtrate but is normally absent from urine. Which substance fits this pattern?

options.text: Glucose
options.why: Glucose is small enough to be ultrafiltered, but it’s normally reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule.

options.text: A red blood cell
options.why: Red blood cells are too large to cross the filtration barrier, so they’re absent from both normal filtrate and urine.

options.text: A large plasma protein
options.why: Most large plasma proteins remain in the blood because the glomerular filtration barrier excludes them.

options.text: Urea
options.why: Urea enters the filtrate and some remains for excretion, so it’s normally present in urine.
